title: Branch Misprediction Visualizer
description: Two pipeline lanes stepping through the same ten branch outcomes, one predictable and one data-dependent, with pipeline flushes and a running wasted-cycle tally.
creator: Real-Time DSP on a $5 Microcontroller
author: Dan McCreary
subject: Digital Signal Processing
Computer Architecture
Assembly Language

educational.topic: Branch prediction and the cost of a pipeline flush
learningObjectives: Explain why a predictable branch costs almost nothing
Interpret a pipeline flush as discarded speculative work
Distinguish the cost of a comparison from the cost of a wrong guess
prerequisites: A pipeline overlaps fetch, decode, and execute
A branch direction is unknown until it executes
Loops end in a conditional branch

controls.label: Step
controls.purpose: Resolve one branch in both lanes simultaneously

controls.label: Reset
controls.purpose: Return both lanes to the unstarted state

simulationModel.modelType: One-bit branch predictor driving two three-stage pipelines over a fixed outcome sequence
equations: predictable sequence = nine taken then one not-taken
unpredictable sequence yields five mispredicts in ten
assumptions: A one-bit predictor, the simplest scheme that still learns a counted loop
A flush discards exactly the Fetch and Decode stages, costing two cycles
Both lanes execute identical instruction sequences apart from the branch outcome
limitations: Real Cortex-M cores use more elaborate prediction and prefetch than a one-bit scheme
Memory stalls, which can dominate in practice, are not modeled

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Side-by-side stepping so the same number of branches produces visibly different costs
keyQuestions: What does the comparison cost, and what does the wrong guess cost?
How does the per-iteration cost of each lane change as the loop gets longer?
commonMisconceptions: That the cost is in evaluating the condition rather than in guessing wrong
assessmentOpportunities: Explain how doing unnecessary arithmetic can make a loop faster
Predict the ten outcomes by hand using the one-bit rule and score the result
